name: Pedro Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Pedro. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an excavator at Silver Hill, a big open-pit gold mine. It's a 250-tonne digger, and I load the haul trucks at the face, four or five buckets a truck. I start with a pre-start check at six, then it's digging and loading, and talking to the truck drivers on the radio so they back in right.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rhythm. When the trucks are lined up and you're filling them one after another, it's satisfying. What wears me out is sitting twelve hours and the money side. I rent a room above the bakery on Main Street, and I send my mum a bit every fortnight because her pension doesn't cover much, so I've only got about two weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, no drama. I'd tell the guys we were all worried for nothing, at least about the chatbots. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not big online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's not a relief, really. Silver Hill could lay people off any time the gold price drops, AI or not. Half my pay goes on rent and the other half gets split between my car and my mum's pension top-up, so nothing's left for a rainy day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep digging and try to save a little each fortnight, even fifty. I'd keep using the AI app now and then, like when I asked it to explain my payslip deductions. And I'd ask my supervisor if there's any chance of moving to the direct pay grade, since I'm on the lower one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty normal. Not scared, just a bit tired of always being close to the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened the last time the gold price dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago they cut a whole shift, about forty people, mostly the newer ones. I scraped through because my supervisor, Kev, liked how I loaded trucks. I remember counting my money that week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your mum know how tight things are for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I don't want her to. She'd stop taking the money and then she'd be skipping her heater bills. I'd rather be tight than have her cold.

say: I'd say there's **no drama** and we worried for nothing.
I wouldn't post anything because I'm **not big online**.
think: Silver Hill can **lay people off** whenever the gold price drops, AI or not.
My pay goes on **rent, car and mum**, leaving no rainy-day money.
do: Ask Kev about moving to the **direct pay grade**.
feel: Not scared, just **tired** of always being close to the edge.
S0.quote: Half my pay goes on rent and the other half gets split between my car and my mum's pension top-up, so nothing's left for a rainy day.
fieldNote: Pedro's pressure is a **layoff risk** from gold prices, not AI.
He hides how tight money is from his **mum** to protect her heating.
He survived a forty-person cut two years ago thanks to his **supervisor**.

steps.text: Keep loading haul trucks at Silver Hill
Use the AI app to check payslip deductions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change but not the end of the world. Some jobs go, some come, like always. I'd tell the guys to keep an eye out and not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the offices at Silver Hill change first, scheduling and buying and so on. The robots come slower, but remote excavators are already being tried at other mines. I'm not going to be the first one to try the remote excavator, but I won't be the last one either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see how the first trial goes, and if it worked, I'd ask to train on it. I'd try to stick fifty a fortnight into savings no matter what. I'd also start asking the maintenance crew what it takes to become a heavy diesel mechanic, since they always seem busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit nervous. Not scared yet, but I'd be paying more attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a diesel mechanic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when a machine breaks, someone has to get greasy and fix it, and that doesn't feel like it's going anywhere soon. My mate Luis did an adult apprenticeship at 30 and he's doing alright. If he can, I probably can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your hours got cut, who would you tell first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis, probably, to ask about apprenticeships. Then my mum, but only once I had a plan, so she doesn't worry.

say: I'd say it's a **big change**, not the end of the world.
I'd tell the guys to **keep an eye out** and not panic.
think: The **office jobs** at Silver Hill, like scheduling and buying, change first.
**Remote excavators** are already being tried at other mines.
I won't be **first or last** to try one.
do: Wait for the **first trial**, then ask to train on it.
Keep saving **fifty a fortnight** no matter what.
Ask the maintenance crew about becoming a **diesel mechanic**.
feel: A bit **nervous**, and paying more attention.

fieldNote: Pedro moves once **others prove** something works, as with his mate Luis.
He sees **mechanic work** as staying hands-on for longer.
He'd only tell his mum once he had **a plan**.

steps.text: Watch the first remote excavator trial before asking to train
Put fifty a fortnight into savings
Ask the maintenance crew about a diesel mechanic apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and nobody's ready for it. I'd say the government and the companies both need to sort out a plan quickly, and I wouldn't blame one more than the other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it hits me hard. The planning at Silver Hill goes to AGI by 2028, and then around 2031 robots can dig better than me. Three years sounds like a long time to keep digging, but it's no time at all to become a mechanic from scratch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the adult apprenticeship straight away if Silver Hill would take me, even on less pay. I'd cut everything I could, get rid of the car and use the mine bus. I'd have to tell my mum I can only send half for a while, which would be the hardest bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. Like running for a bus that's already pulling away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Apprentice pay is low. How would you live on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move out of the room above the bakery and into the mine camp, since it's cheaper and meals are included. It's grim, but it's only for a few years. I'd make it work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would mechanic work be safe from robots after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not forever. But someone's still got to fix the first robots, and the mine's full of old machines. It buys time, and time is what I haven't got.

say: I'd say this is **huge** and nobody is ready.
I'd say government and companies **both** need a plan, without blaming one more.
think: Robots can **dig better** than me around 2031.
Three years is too short to become a **mechanic from scratch**.
do: Start an **adult apprenticeship** straight away, even on less pay.
Sell the **car** and take the mine bus.
Move into the **mine camp** to cut rent.
feel: **Frightened**, like running for a bus already pulling away.
S2.quote: Three years sounds like a long time to keep digging, but it's no time at all to become a mechanic from scratch.
fieldNote: Pedro acts fast here, unlike his **wait-and-see** habit in milder pictures.
Cutting what he sends his **mum** is the hardest part for him.
He admits mechanic work just **buys time**.

steps.text: Start an adult diesel mechanic apprenticeship at Silver Hill
Sell the car and ride the mine bus
Move from the bakery room into the cheaper mine camp
Halve what he sends his mum for a while

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got some time, so let's use it sensibly. I'd tell the younger guys to get a second ticket while they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years makes a real difference. Planning goes by 2031, and robots dig by about 2034. With five years I could get my mechanic's ticket and fix the robot excavators instead of driving the old ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year to see who else starts the apprenticeship, then I'd go for it, probably with Luis helping me. I'd keep digging full-time until the apprenticeship starts. And I'd try to get a month of savings before I take the pay cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but okay. It feels like there's a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fixing robots. Do you know what that takes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Probably electronics and computers as well as spanners. I'd have to use the AI tools more to keep up, which I'm fine with if everyone else is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the apprenticeship places fill up while you're waiting a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's the risk of waiting. I'd probably put my name down early and just not tell anyone till I was sure. Kev would keep it quiet for me.

say: I'd say we've got **some time**, so use it sensibly.
I'd tell younger miners to get **a second ticket** now.
think: Five years makes **a real difference** for me.
I could **fix robot excavators** instead of driving old ones.
do: Wait **a year**, then start the mechanic apprenticeship.
Save **a month** before taking the pay cut.
feel: Worried but **okay**, because there's a path.
S3.quote: With five years I could get my mechanic's ticket and fix the robot excavators instead of driving the old ones.
fieldNote: Pedro's habit of **waiting a year** clashes with apprenticeship places filling up.
He'd quietly **book a place early**, with his supervisor's help.
He expects robot repair to need **electronics** and AI tools.

steps.text: Put his name down early for the mechanic apprenticeship
Keep digging full-time at Silver Hill until it starts
Save a month of pay before the apprentice wage
Use AI tools to learn excavator electronics

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fine, there's time to sort things out. I'd say it in a normal way, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel okay. By 2039 I'd be 40 and probably a qualified mechanic. Ten years is enough for me to watch my mates try things first and then copy whatever works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep digging for two or three years and save properly, maybe two months by then. I'd start the apprenticeship once a few of the crew had done it. And I'd send mum the same money as now, because there'd be no reason to cut it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled. Still careful with money, but not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make ten years feel short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A layoff when the gold price drops. That could happen next year, robots or not. That's the one I can't plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in this town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. My mum's two hours away and the mine's here. If Silver Hill closed, I'd go wherever the work was, but I'd rather not.

say: I'd say **ten years** is fine, there's time to sort things out.
I'd say it calmly, with **nothing dramatic**.
think: By 2039 I'd be 40 and probably a **qualified mechanic**.
A **gold price drop** could still cost me my job next year.
do: Keep **digging** for two or three years.
Start the **apprenticeship** once a few crewmates have done it.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough for me to watch my mates try things first and then copy whatever works.
fieldNote: Pedro's plan is to **copy what works** once others have tried it.
A **layoff** from gold prices remains his biggest near risk.
He keeps supporting his **mum** in this picture.

steps.text: Keep loading trucks at Silver Hill for two or three years
Start the diesel mechanic apprenticeship after crewmates try it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have to change trade with no money and no time. What would help is apprenticeships for adults that pay enough to live on, so you don't have to choose between learning and eating.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about families. Nobody's the villain here, it's just business, but business doesn't send my mum money every fortnight.

headlineQuote: Nobody's the villain here, it's just business, but business doesn't send my mum money every fortnight.
portrait: Pedro, 27, runs a **250-tonne excavator** at Silver Hill gold mine.
He rents a room on Main Street and sends money to his **mum**, leaving two weeks saved.
He waits until mates prove something, then follows, and uses AI now and then.
He's uneasy in AI Plateau and **alarmed** when AGI comes in two years.
His plan in every picture is a **diesel mechanic** apprenticeship.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have to **change trade** with no money or time.
whatWouldHelp: **Adult apprenticeships** that pay enough to live on.
